Brunch
BRUNCH
noun (Millennial slang)
A blend of breakfast and lunch, first proposed in print by Guy Beringer in the British magazine Hunter’s Weekly in 1895 ("Brunch: A Plea"), as a late Sunday meal for people who had been out on Saturday night. It became an American restaurant institution in the twentieth century and a defining Millennial ritual in the 2010s: weekend reservations, bottomless mimosas, eggs Benedict, avocado toast, and photographs of all of it.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Brunch is the late, leisurely weekend meal between breakfast and lunch, and for Millennials it became something like a weekly ritual: friends, a long table, mimosas, eggs, conversation, and photos. The Christian observation: much about brunch is good. Scripture loves tables. The early church "continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart" (Act 2:46). Jesus ate a breakfast of fish and bread with His disciples on the shore after His resurrection: "Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine" (Joh 21:12). Friendship around food is a gift. But the Millennial brunch has a calendar problem: it happens on Sunday mornings, when the Lord’s people gather to worship. Beringer invented it for those recovering from Saturday night, and its modern form, with "bottomless" drinks at noon, often competes directly with the Lord’s Day. Scripture calls the people of God to that day: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is" (Heb 10:25). There is also the question of excess; Proverbs warns that "the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty" (Pro 23:21). A father can take his family to brunch after church and make it a feast of thanksgiving, and teach his children that the Lord’s table and the Lord’s people come first, and the eggs Benedict can wait an hour.

Webster 1828 Definition

A 1895 coinage (Guy Beringer) for the late breakfast-lunch, turned Millennial weekend ritual (2010s); table fellowship is biblical (Act 2:46; Joh 21:12), but the Sunday brunch often displaces the Lord’s Day assembly (Heb 10:25).

BRUNCH, n. (1895; Millennial weekend ritual, 2010s) A late-morning meal combining breakfast and lunch, often on weekends with friends. Culture: bottomless mimosas, avocado toast, brunch photos.

Webster (1828), root lunch: LUNCH, LUNCH ’EON, noun Literally, a swallow; but in usage, a portion of food taken at any time, except at a regular meal. It is not unusual to take a luncheon before dinner. The passengers in the line-ships regularly have their lunch I sliced the luncheon from the barley loaf.

Decode for parents: brunch after church is a feast; brunch instead of church is a choice about what Sunday is for.

Key Scripture

Act 2:46 — "And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,"

Joh 21:12 — "Jesus saith unto them, Come and dine. And none of the disciples durst ask him, Who art thou? knowing that it was the Lord."

Heb 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

Pro 23:21 — "For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags."

Psa 118:24 — "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it."

Modern Corruption

Brunch is good table fellowship, but as a Sunday-morning sacrament it often replaces the Lord’s Day assembly; Scripture puts worship first and feasting after.

expand to see more

The corruption is in the calendar and the liturgy. Brunch took Sunday morning, the hour Christians had for centuries given to worship, and filled it with a secular ritual of rest, friendship, and indulgence. It is not hard to see why a generation drifting from the church found brunch a satisfying replacement: it offers community, a weekly rhythm, and a sense of the good life. But it is a table without a Lord. The bottomless mimosa adds the old danger of drunkenness to the morning.

The redemption is to restore the order. "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it" (Psa 118:24): first the assembly, the Word, the Lord’s Supper; then the long table with friends and family, the best food of the week, and laughter. Christians should be the people who make Sunday lunch an event. Teach the young to love both tables, in the right order.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Breakfast + lunch → brunch (Beringer, Hunter’s Weekly, 1895) → 20th-c. American restaurant custom → 2010s Millennial ritual.

Breakfast (to break the fast) + lunch (a portion of food)

1895: Guy Beringer, "Brunch: A Plea," Hunter’s Weekly

20th c.: American hotels and restaurants adopt Sunday brunch

2010s: Millennial ritual; mimosas, avocado toast, photographs

Biblical anchor: breaking bread from house to house (Act 2:46); Come and dine (Joh 21:12)

Usage

""Brunch Sunday at eleven?""

"Come and dine (Joh 21:12): Christ’s own breakfast with His friends."

"Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together (Heb 10:25): church first, then brunch."
